items.body: Some records ask to be heard; Philippe Petit’s Lightning Field 01. Constraint asks to be observed, documenting the unpredictable conversation between composer, electricity, and machine at the heart of modular synthesis. Fragments of a larger ongoing investigation Modulisme Session 144. Lightning Field 01. Constraint by Philippe Petit   Modular synthesis releases occupy a deeply specific and persistently misunderstood territory within experimental electronic music—a territory that operates by entirely different rules than those governing conventional recorded sound. These aren’t listening experiences in the expected sense. They’re dispatches. Evidence gathered from the interior of a process most listeners will never witness directly. A conversation conducted between a composer and a system that has its own grammar, its own tolerance for deviation, its own appetite for accident. The best of them carry no trace of manufacture. They feel discovered rather than designed, unearthed from the space between human decision and machine response. At its most essential, the modular release functions less like composition and more like field recording, the distinction being that the field here is electrical, the landscape assembled from patch cables, voltage gradients, and the irreducible uncertainty that lives in the gap between what a composer instructs and what a system chooses to return. Modulisme—the platform born in July 2019 out of Marseille, described as a media documenting left-field modular synthesis, has been building this archive since its inception, reaching session 144 here. The platform operates like a library rather than a label, curating exclusive one-hour sessions from composers working with modular systems across the full range of the form, from academic electroacoustic tradition through to experimental improvisation and everything in between. By session 144, the catalog represents over a thousand exclusive works and a genuine document of where modular synthesis composition stands in the mid-2020s. The artist behind Modulisme is Philippe Petit himself—a Marseille-born composer, DJ, label operator, and self-described “musical travel agent” who has been releasing work since 2000 across labels including Sub Rosa, Monotype, Home Normal, Staubgold, and his own BiP_HOp imprint, which from 2000 to 2010 advocated left-field electronica before eventually becoming Modulisme. He studied electroacoustic music at the CNRR Conservatory, specializing in multi-channeled diffusion and modular synthesis, working with Buchla System 200, Serge 73/75, and a modified EMS Synthi A. His catalog includes collaborations with Lydia Lunch, Edward Ka-Spel, Eugene S. Robinson, and a genuinely vast network of experimental musicians accumulated over decades of restless cross-genre activity. He describes himself not as a composer but as someone who transmigrates source material, an apt description for an artist whose work has always been about the movement between forms rather than the forms themselves. Electricity itself as the subject rather than a medium :: Lightning Field 01. Constraint is the first volume of a new series in which Petit imposes a specific limitation on himself: no acoustic instruments, no vocals, no field recordings. The usual escape routes he describes reaching for in composition—a piano frame, a prepared guitar, voices, found sounds, are deliberately removed. What remains is his Buchla and Serge systems working in isolation, and the results of letting those systems define the boundaries of what’s possible. The title is precise, this is a volume about the founding decision, the acceptance of voluntary limitation, and what that limitation reveals. It’s the same constraint logic that has driven the most interesting experimental music for decades, from Alvin Lucier‘s single-premise compositions to the Oulipo literary movement’s rule-based writing. What happens when you remove the familiar? What surfaces in the space left behind? What surfaces here is a series of works that treat electricity itself as the subject rather than a medium. Petit describes the modular as a miniature weather system whose internal architecture has been laid bare, not an instrument but a machine for intimate storms. That’s not marketing language. It’s an accurate description of how Buchla and Serge systems behave in the hands of someone who understands their particular logic. Unlike Eurorack, which tends toward precision and control, the Buchla and Serge traditions lean toward instability, drift, and the productive unpredictability of analog voltage. A patch on a Buchla system creates relationships between modules that interact and evolve in ways that can’t be fully predicted in advance. The composer sets conditions rather than issuing instructions. What emerges from those conditions is the work. The tracks themselves are labeled in iterations: “Field 04,” “Field 05,” “Field 06,” and so on, through to “Field 15.” Each one is a short burst of electronic bubbles and modular clicks, some containing feedback, others carrying rhythm. They function less as tracks in the conventional sense and more as specimens, individual electrical events captured and named sequentially rather than titled descriptively. That naming convention is itself a statement about what these pieces are. They’re not songs. They’re not compositions in the way that word is usually understood. They’re fragments of a larger ongoing investigation, numbered because they occurred in an order, not because they need to be experienced in one. This recalls the classic modular sessions of the 1970s and 80s, the early Moog explorations of Wendy Carlos, whose Switched-On Bach (1968) introduced the synthesizer to mainstream audiences but whose later works like Sonic Seasonings (1972) pushed into more abstract, atmospheric territory. Klaus Schulze‘s extended Berlin School synthesizer pieces, Tangerine Dream‘s Phaedra and Rubycon, Morton Subotnick‘s Silver Apples of the Moon (1967)—the first electronic work commissioned by a record label, and the musique concrète lineage running through Pierre Henry and Bernard Parmegiani at INA/GRM in Paris all share the same fundamental question Petit is asking here: what does electricity sound like when you stop trying to make it sound like something else? The longest track in the batch is “Field 06,” running at 11:08, and it’s the most melodic of the bunch. It opens with a sequence arp cycling through different tones, rhythms going off-tone and on again, speeds shifting, different oscillators being introduced and withdrawn. More than any other piece here it plays on the melodic and rhythmic side of modular synthesis—the arp becoming a kind of unstable melody, never quite resolving, always pointing somewhere it doesn’t arrive. Much of what’s played throughout the series sits in distortions and rhythms rather than conventional melodic structure, which is consistent with Petit‘s stated intention to let the systems generate the conditions rather than imposing a compositional outcome on top of them. This is not for the casual listener. That needs to be stated plainly. You won’t find structural familiarity here, no verse-chorus logic, no emotional arc that announces itself. These are pieces, not tracks, electrical specimens, experiments in what a Buchla and Serge system will produce when given a set of conditions and allowed to follow its own logic. This is Session 144, and the fact that it’s Petit‘s own session rather than a guest is significant. He built this platform to document the modular synthesis community and has spent years giving that platform to others. Turning the session on himself, and specifically doing so under a constraint he describes as deliberate, as a way of denying himself the usual escape routes, suggests this isn’t a casual exercise. Lightning Field is announced as a series, meaning this first volume of constraint is the beginning of something longer and more sustained. Not obsessively themed, but genuinely exploratory, each volume investigating the same territory from a different angle, the synthesizer as an active field through which forces circulate rather than a machine that produces predetermined outcomes. For an artist who has spent over two decades documenting what other people do with electricity and cables and voltage, this is Petit finally turning the recording equipment on himself and letting his own storm be captured. The sound is no longer manufactured. It is, as he writes, captured. Guided. Transmuted. Whether that transmutation continues to reveal new territory across future Lightning Field volumes is the question worth watching. Session 144 makes a compelling case that it will. Modulisme Session 144. Lightning Field 01. Constraint is available on Modulisme. [Bandcamp] Modulisme Session 144. Lightning Field 01. items.body: The finest quality of Ladybug 1 comes from its ability to treat dub as an art of emotional memory. Each return of the theme seems to erase something and make it more vivid at the same time. In the leaner versions, rhythm becomes a heavy step through smoke, reverbs widen like liquid metal, silences speak with the same intensity as the impacts. Vanishing is the core and the fate of the whole EP Ladybug 1 by The Bug / Dis Fig   With Ladybug 1 EP, Kevin Richard Martin opens the Ladybug series on Pressure through a work of emotional precision. Each chapter will bring a different female voice into his bass universe, and the first presence is Dis Fig, Felicia Chen, already a crucial companion on In Blue (Hyperdub). The memory of that album returns like a call from the dark, and here the step shifts, the air grows warmer, the pulse slows, the matter turns more bodily. The Bug has shaped, across decades, a language immediately his own, born from dub, dancehall, industrial music, spectral hip hop, sound system devotion and lab fever. Chen comes from another fire, formed through noise culture, club practice, wounded vocality and physical performance. Together they find a zone where song becomes atmospheric pressure, and dub moves from genre into inner weather. Vanishing is the core and the fate of the whole EP. Around the main piece, versions, dubs and deeper immersions expand the same emotional event, as Martin opens the body of the music and reveals nerves, vapor, rhythmic apparatus, magnetic blood. The choice moves beyond the simple idea of a remix set and takes on an almost cinematic form: one ghost seen from different angles, one trauma changing density at every pass. The bass carries the weight of a horizon drawing near, pushing from below, bending the light. The percussion advances slowly, with the authority of a machine that knows the measure of pain. Around it, ambient trails, dub vapors, shoegaze reflections and exhausted sensuality gather into music that feels vast, physical, tender in its devastation. It is dub for the end of love, soul for immense systems, electronics speaking to the body before thought. A series debut with the force of something necessary: a handful of tracks, a single emotional center, a depth that grows with every listen. ~Mirco Salvadori Dis Fig’s singing is the point where this mass receives a face. Her voice descends along the lines of sound, melts into the kick, then rises again like a private confession caught by an apparatus far too powerful. The lyrics, written by Chen, seem to follow disappearance after a romantic rupture: the loss of the loved body, the numbness after impact, desire continuing to send signals after contact has faded. The word Vanishing becomes gesture, phenomenon, progressive erasure, almost a way of naming the fading of the self inside the echo of another. Chen sings with feverish grace, close to secular prayer and stripped soul, letting fragility, narcotic sweetness, muted resentment and burning lucidity pass through. Her presence turns the brutality of the low end into feeling, gives the machine a human breath, carries the wound to the center of the system. The finest quality of Ladybug 1 comes from its ability to treat dub as an art of emotional memory. Each return of the theme seems to erase something and make it more vivid at the same time. In the leaner versions, rhythm becomes a heavy step through smoke, reverbs widen like liquid metal, silences speak with the same intensity as the impacts. Martin’s hand knows the tradition of the mixing desk as creative instrument, the lesson of Scientist, the daring of On U Sound, the hypnotic depth of Basic Channel, the mutant melancholy of King Midas Sound. Here those lines enter a new tale, more feverish and sentimental, where sound system culture meets a broken ballad, lover’s rock is projected into a digital night, and Massive Attack appears as a distant memory filtered through exhausted subwoofers. Ladybug 1 chooses concentration. Each impact carries weight, each halo has narrative function, each sonic ghost guides listening toward a feeling of separation that becomes a mental landscape. ~Mirco Salvadori The strength of the brief format lies in its visionary economy. Five passages, a single title changing skin, a progression shaped through subtraction and fever, with the sound seeming to grow larger as ornament falls away. Martin sculpts low air with the patience of a craftsman and the fury of an engineer of controlled collapse; Chen cuts a melodic line across the surface of the magma, curving, trembling, touching silence, then rising again with an almost soul like grace. In a moment when much contemporary music confuses intensity with accumulation, Ladybug 1 chooses concentration. Each impact carries weight, each halo has narrative function, each sonic ghost guides listening toward a feeling of separation that becomes a mental landscape. Ladybug 1 therefore works as a miniature manifesto. It introduces a future series and says plenty about the present of The Bug: the urgency to keep collaborating, to offer his architecture of pressure to voices able to carry risk, desire and biography. For Dis Fig, this return feels like another change of state: from the floating presence of In Blue to a dominant emotional figure, able to bend Martin’s matter toward an abstract blues for saturated times. The music moves slowly, sensually, menacingly, with a beauty born from compression more than explosion. It is dub for the end of love, soul for immense systems, electronics speaking to the body before thought. A series debut with the force of something necessary: a handful of tracks, a single emotional center, a depth that grows with every listen. Ladybug 1 is available on Pressure. items.body: “Qué Loquera”, roughly “What Madness”, is a merengue-driven satire of a planet cooking itself, and of the lovesick singer going down with it. As the world falls apart, Nene del Solar reaches for aguapacheo, his word for wet-kissing on the dancefloor, as the way to carry the grief of man-made catastrophe. The song runs deconstructed Caribbean rhythms, digital synthesisers and chanted onomatopoeia into salsa tumbaos rewired for the dancefloor. It takes the dance straight through the madness of its title, and its AI-generated video turns the tool on itself, a direct hit at artificial intelligence, tech-bros and the way digital life burns through the planet, made by Fabián Mosele and Ali Bardavid. That mix of homemade tropical machines and end-of-the-world dread puts the track in the frame of Caribbean futurism: speculative art that faces down climate collapse and the plunder of the Global South from the region’s own rhythms and beliefs, keeping the machines and dropping the worship of them. The single opens Donde Hay Calor, the debut album from Nene del Solar, released on 17 July through In-Correcto, the Bogotá collective and label that has spent a decade gathering the city’s cumbia, rap, folk and electronic outliers.   Behind the alias is Icaro Lopez de Mesa Moyano, a Colombian sound-media artist who builds the motorised percussion he plays and calls it Los Robots del Ritmo. He works between Bogotá and Bremen, where he is a doctoral candidate, with eight years of traditional Latin American music training behind him, an industrial design degree from Colombia’s National University and a digital media masters from Germany. His projects have played Rock Al Parque at home and SXSW in Texas. Stream “Qué Loquera” HERE and pick up your copy of Donde Hay Calor following THIS LINK The post Daily Discovery: Nene del Solar – Qué Loquera appeared first on Rhythm Passport.

"Can I Tell You" is the opening track from this unique violin-led band?a gritty, rhythmic rock number sitting somewhere between classic and symphonic rock; a fresh experience delivering explosive rock energy.2. "Bringing It Back" kicks off with boogie-woogie piano; the violin and Robbie's vocals drive an energetic, swirling groove. A new sound is born here?one that's hard to pin down to specific influences because it feels entirely original.3. "Lonely Wind" features piano and vocals, with Steve sharing lead duties; note Phil's delicate touch and Kerry's warm keyboards on this killer slow ballad.4. "Belexes" arrives with high-energy keyboards engaging in a musical duel. The melody flows like glowing embers tumbling down a slope; the organ is on fire?fittingly so?and the backing vocals are in full swing. Rich, sporting his signature headband, delivers a sharp, high-pitched guitar solo, cementing the band's trademark blend of keyboards, guitar, and violin. The track heats up further with a final drum solo that sets the listener's ears ablaze.5. "Journey From Mariabronn" is the first of three epic-length tracks; with its violin variations and piano melody, I detect a nod to Supertramp. The song bears a progressive stamp reminiscent of Queen, while the keyboards evoke Yes?heavy stuff! Dave's bass anchors everything and drives the momentum; in short, a magnificent piece of prog rock.6. "The Pilgrimage" returns to a blend of pop, rock, folk, and boogie with a touch of Southern rock flair?thanks to the violin and backing vocals?though it's a bit too brief to truly hook the listener.7. "Apercu" offers a more substantial experience, opening with a spirited energy that leads into verses shared by the two frontmen. The violin ushers in an instrumental section with clear folk undertones, infusing the music with a festive spirit?a fantastic glimpse into their fusion of rock and symphonic styles. The finale takes on an elegiac tone, introduced by a solemn violin before shifting into heavy?or rather hard?rock, driven by the sheer power of the drums and guitar; this intensity carries over into the next track:8. "Death Of Mother Nature Suite," a true grand finale for this distinctive debut album. Here, heavy rock weightiness blends with a melancholic violin. The song navigates shifting harmonic textures, balancing tender sensitivity with the fiery power of the chorus?where the backing vocals truly shine. The guitar solo serves as an immediate reminder that Kansas is a band of the highest caliber. It was undoubtedly a stunning achievement for the genre of folk-infused heavy rock.

items.body: Review by Circuito_Prog — With Pestkr�nikene, Jordsj� celebrates its tenth anniversary without relying on easy nostalgia. Even though the album is built from material written between 2020 and 2025, the Norwegian duo gives it a strong identity and a cohesive concept centered on war, the fall of ancient kingdoms, religious fanaticism, and rebuilding after devastation. Rather than feeling like a collection of leftovers, it stands as one of the band's most cohesive releases.Musically, Jordsj� reinforces the sound that has made them one of the leading names in modern Scandinavian progressive rock. The analog warmth of the production, the prominent use of flute, vintage keyboards, and the balance between pastoral passages and heavier moments create a distinctly Nordic atmosphere. You'll hear echoes of Jethro Tull, Wobbler, �nglag�rd, and even touches of Gentle Giant or Anekdoten, but the band never loses its own identity.One of the album's greatest strengths is how much it accomplishes in just 35 minutes. In a genre often dominated by sprawling epics, Jordsj� opts for compact compositions, most of them between three and five minutes long, keeping the album moving at a steady pace without ever feeling overstuffed. That brevity occasionally makes a few ideas seem to end a little too soon, but it also makes Pestkr�nikene an engaging listen that rewards repeated plays with its intricate details.The guest appearances by Jon A. Henriksen, Andreas Prestmo, and Lars Fredrik Fr�islie add plenty of depth without overshadowing the creative partnership of H�kon Oftung and Kristian Fr�land. Each musician brings something unique to the record, while the production maintains the organic, handcrafted feel that sets it apart from many contemporary releases.Pestkr�nikene doesn't reinvent progressive rock, but it proves there's still plenty of room to expand its boundaries while staying rooted in tradition. It's an album filled with rich atmospheres, memorable melodies, and carefully crafted arrangements that further establishes Jordsj� as one of the most consistent bands in today's European progressive rock scene. It may not reach the grand scale of some of the genre's biggest landmarks, but its authenticity, balance, and genuine love for classic progressive rock make it one of the most worthwhile releases of 2026. items.body: Review by alainPP — Hawkestrel is Alan Davey releasing this 17th opus, distilling the energy of his diverse body of work. Tracks spanning space rock, prog, psych, jazz, and metal, featuring guest artists and original band members. A collection of sensational Hawkwind covers alongside reworkings of songs by Led Zeppelin, the Beach Boys, and Cream."Hall of the Mountain Grill"?featuring piano and flute?is a 1974 track where I find myself desperately searching for Grieg's influence. It is a dark cover, enhanced by Simon's brooding violin. "Brainstorm" channels a Murkey Red vibe?a wild, stoner-punk-psych hybrid blending thick synth, violin, and sax into an apoplectic maelstrom. "Rainbow Demon," an Uriah Heep cover, delivers the organ and riffs of an era before "hard rock" even had a name; Mick's shimmering guitar evokes a vintage feel that invites a nostalgic trip back in time. "Sunshine of Your Love" resurrects Cream's raw, unadorned sound?Ginger's drumming and that vibrant riff flirting with gritty, snarling rock. "Children of the Sun" transports us back to 1971; a heavy riff meets fiery violin, creating a driving track that surfs on psychedelic clouds. Del lets his synth spiral wildly?a touch of Hawkwind meets Ozric Tentacles. "Subterraneans" features vocals reminiscent of Bowie's Robert-era style and a reverberating atmosphere?proto-space-rock "fudge" ahead of its time. Notes swirl, soaking the track in the nascent vibe of early space rock; it ends with an airplane-style outro."Black Dog" features female vocals and Keith's keyboards bursting joyfully out of the solar system?a rhythmic psychedelic cover. "Starcruiser" stands out for its intro?just the way I like it?with Michael's distinctive voice driving a frenetic psych-rock track filled with swirling, wind-like synth sounds. "The Greenfly and The Rose" sees Michael continuing the set, accompanied by a medieval-sounding organ. The drift continues?a pre-emptive stutter of cold wave, pompous art-rock, and Southern rock?floating through cottony limbo. "The Cairene Purse" unfolds over a *Flash Gordon*-esque synth line, a narrative interlude transporting the listener elsewhere to explore a story born of the artist's imagination. "Good Vibrations" is revisited through a psychedelic lens, evoking the latent atmosphere of a parallel universe?as if the Beach Boys had truly conceived the track as a prog-psych-rock testament in the vein of Hawkwind.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A Dutch blues-rock jam band who aspired to Kosmische-style jazz-rock music and, in fact, notably were successful at creating their own particular kind of jazz-rock music while coming from Traffic- and The Who-like blues-rock perspectives.1. "Saras Ritt Durch Schwarzwald" (6:23) impressive Who-like Rock approaching Hawkwind-like Prog or Krautrock. I love Johannes Pappert's Arabian/Indian-styled sax play in the fourth and fifth minute's "interlude." The singing (in Dutch) is like a cross between CAN and early Ozzie. (8.75/10)2. "M.C. Escher" (6:14) the organ-base to the first minute of this one makes it feel like URIAH HEEP but then Johannes' sax enters, taking the wind out of the heavy rock vibe. At the end of the second minute the music totally changes (though still using the same instrumental palette): driving rock drums and bass with long-sustained organ chords. A reliance on a set "heavy metal" guitar chord progression is also reminiscent of bands like Heep, Sabbath, Deep Purple, and Nektar. A brief "normal" voiced lyric in the middle is interesting for its educational attempt. (8.6667/10)3. "Kraan Arabia" (9:45) another droning near-"heavy metal" song that is so quintessentially Krautrock is most notable for the way it exploits Johannes' Arabian sounding and melodic sensibilities on his saxophone. There are a couple sound effects switches on the sax and a few windows for Peter Wolbrandt's rhythm guitar and lead guitar to step into the spotlight. And, damn! Hellmut Hattler is a solid and yet fluid bass player. Note the flange effect placed upon the mics recording Jan Fride's cymbals. The laughter and "smoke-break" breakdown in the eighth minute is rather FOCUS- and CAN-like but it also enables Hellmut the chance to solo a bit (not as good of a soloist as rhythmatist) as well as Jan to show off his conga and supplemental percussion instrumental skills while also showcasing more of Peter's guitar skills (also a great rhythmatist). (17.75/20)4. "Head" (18:36) impressive display of rhythmic expression and group unity--especially from Hellmut and Jan. Too bad about the somewhat cheesy riffs borrowed from British rockers like The Who. (35.5/40)5. "Sara auf der Gansewies" (2:01) bluesy cinema music using sax and guitar doubled up to present the plaintive main melody and bass. I like it though it is nothing Earth-shatteringly innovative. (4.375/5)Total Time: 42:59A rock album that draws from a lot of diverse influences including a Krautrock foundation that is heavily steeped in Can-like Kosmische Musik, Steve Winwood organ-based Blues-Rock, The Who's new and more concise Rock 'n' Roll, Chicago Transit Authority jazz-rock, and many of the psychedelic influences that tap into (or arise from) Middle Eastern and Oriental influences. It is also obvious that the band had heard Can, King Crimson, Brainbox/Focus, The Who, and The Mahavishnu Orchestra. Despite their jazzification of a lot of their instrumental performances, the music here feels quite solidly founded in blues-rock structures and motifs--which makes them feel much more akin to bands like The Spencer Davis Group and Traffic. They may have been inspired by The Mahavishnu Orchestra but they sound to me much more like Ash Ra Tempel, Amon D��l II, and/or Can. And, yes: Hellmut Hattler is a GREAT bass player! (How 'bout bringing he and Can's Jaki Liebezeit together with Triumvirat's J�rgen Fritz and Jan Akkerman for a Teutonic super super-group!)B-/3.5 stars; a nice addition to any prog rocker's music collection--especially if s/he is interested in the early foundational music of Krautrock, European Heavy Metal, and/or psychedelic prog.

items.body: Review by BrufordFreak — A London-based band of musicians expressing their Afro-Caribbean roots through Anglo-American psychedelic Soul/R&B.A1. "Zion I" (3:27) despite the Afro-Jamaican roots being expressed here, there is a laid-back sophistication here that predicts the direction that the band WAR would be taking in a couple years. (8.875/10)A2. "One More" (3:04) more laid back Afro-Caribbean sounds that incorporate bagpipe-like sounding instrument into the mix (as a kind of background reinforcer of the main guitar melody during the "choruses"). Satisfying if not fully developed: more like a little warm-up jam or �tude. (8.75/10)A3. "Getting It Back" (4:17) a bit of the drama of The Undisputed Truth and Nina Simone present in both the music and vocal performance. The horns are little too unified, harmonized too synchronically, even though the sax gets to break free and solo a bit in the final minute. (8.6667/10)A4. "Listen" (4:39) another song whose foundation sounds like it's informed by the current trends in American Soul/R&B being by Stax and Motown bands like Ike & Tina Turner, The Staples Singers, and the new kids on the block, The Undisputed Truth. A little boring with its endlessly repeating bass and melody lines. (8.6667/10)A5. "Rickshaw" (5:53) a motif that feels as if it carries over some of the worldly amalgamations achieved at the end of the 1960s by film soundtrack composers like Henry Mancini (Blake Edwards films), Burt Bacharach, and even Eric Burdon's War ("Spill the Wine"). (8.875/10)B1. "Dove" (10:52) a psychedelic jazz-blues jam that sounds like it came straight from San Francisco (Love, Santana, even a little of The Doors) Really nice, satisfying SANTANA-like jam with great groove and lead guitar work from Patrick Patterson. (18.25/20)B2. "Bra" (5:03) more Stax Studios-like Soul/R&B music with a catchy lyric sung in choral chant style. Great bass, drums, rhythm guitar groove with perfect brass section arrangements. (9.125/10)B3. "The Message" (4:19) one of the band's more popular tunes--both as an anthem and as a concert crowd-pleaser. It's a little simple and rather monotonous but apparently the words have significance that draw people in. (8.75/10)B4. "Rastafarian Folk Song" (3:09) exhibiting as fact that not all Jamaican or Rastafarian music is or has to be registered/rendered as Reggae music. Well presented as both engaging music as well as educational fodder. (8.875/10)Total Time 44:43What I hear here is a band who feels that it is their mission to unify African and Caribbean musical traditions with the Soul and Rhythm & Blues of the United States--to open the minds of Anglo-Americans to the interracial trends toward blending and fusion that had been emerging with the 1960s Civil Rights Movement and Anti-War, anti-establishment, counter-cultural revolution.B/four stars; a nice collection of fairly simple Afro-Caribbean Soul/R&B that has two highlight songs. I'd consider this more proto-prog than straightforward prog, Jazz-Rock, or J-R Fusion.

items.body: Label: International Anthem / Nonesuch Records, 2026 Personnel - Jeff Parker: guitar, electronics; Josh Johnson: alto saxophone, electronics; Anna Butterss: bass; Jay Bellerose: drums, percussion. Chicago-based guitarist and bandleader Jeff Parker, a member of the post-rock band Tortoise and the Chicago Underground Trio as well as a sought-after sideman—having worked with Rob Mazurek, Joshua Abrams, Makaya McCraven, and, more recently, Flea—returns with his ETA IVtet project, featuring saxophonist Josh Johnson, bassist Anna Butterss, and drummer Jay Bellerose. Recorded live at the Lodge Room in Los Angeles, Happy Today features two long-form improvised tracks where the group demonstrates unfailing communication while organically exploring well-structured, static spaces. “ Like Swimwear ” starts off with a 16-beat-cycle guitar riff and patiently expands through understated bass maneuvers, micro-detailed saxophone fluctuations that evolve into spiritual Coltrane-like staccatos, and delicate, never obtrusive drum work. Parker designs chromatic figures up and down the fretboard, while Bellerose shifts the rhythmic feel, drawing positive reactions from the audience. Johnson responds with circular movements on his effects-drenched saxophone. A few minutes later, Butterss sets a new groove, and Parker responds with a long-toned, flickering chord that supports the ambient if grooving atmosphere. By the end, the band injects a bluesy feel, gently fusing soul-jazz sensitivity with affable psychedelia. Immersed in these grooving atmospheres, the group eschews outbursts in favor of circularity and speech-inflected long tones, keeping their ears wide open and making decisions in the moment. This is especially noticeable on the title track, “ Happy Today ”, where they seep into the listener’s consciousness with a sustained chord, sparse bass commentary, and soaring saxophone lines before adding tumbling toms, rattling percussion, and shimmering cymbal washes. A six-beat groove is topped by a guitar riff, with Bellerose opting for a backbeat-driven pulse over which Parker’s snake-charmer-like phrases unfold until they exhaust their possibilities. It all ends with a fine pulse in five outlined by Johnson. Happy Today ’s low-key charm is rewarding for those willing to cool down in its waters. Favorite Track: 02 - Happy Today

items.body:
After weeks of fan speculation, LE SSERAFIM have officially confirmed where they'll be performing in Singapore.

The five-piece K-pop girl group will bring their 28 November PUREFLOW world tour stop to the newly launched Apex @ EXPO, confirming what many fans had been anticipating since the group's Asia tour dates were first announced.

The venue reveal comes just over two months after LE SSERAFIM unveiled Singapore as one of the key stops on their 2026 Asia leg, alongside Taipei, Manila and Macau.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by iMe SG 🇸🇬 (@ime.sg)

LE SSERAFIM among the first wave of artists set to perform at Apex @ EXPO, Singapore's newest large-scale live entertainment venue.

With a reported capacity of up to 9,000 attendees, the purpose-built space is poised to become a new stop on the touring circuit, bridging the gap between theatres and arena-sized venues. As international acts continue to include Singapore on their Asia itineraries, Apex @ EXPO offers promoters another mid-sized option that could help accommodate the growing demand for live entertainment in the city.

LE SSERAFIM's concert is expected to be one of the venue's biggest K-pop events to date, signalling the beginning of what could be a busy run of concerts as Apex @ EXPO establishes itself on Singapore's live events calendar.

A post shared by Singapore EXPO (@singaporeexpo)

items.body:
“The thing about playing the tuba in an orchestra is that you don’t have to play that much,” admitted composer Matthew Wright, who grew up playing the tuba in orchestras and funk bands, “but it’s the best seat in the house. You hear music back to front. The percussion and the brass are loud, so you hear all their detail, and the strings are this kind of ethereal thing that’s off in the distance.”

For the Kent-based Wright, who also improvises using turntables, samplers, and processers – most impactfully with Trance Map, his partnership with Evan Parker – this early realization nurtured a sensibility leading to the creation of immersive works that mix composition, improvisation, and technology. Cracked Glaze (False Walls) is a case in point, as it utilizes notated material – “dot music” is his good-humored term – improvisation, and Wright’s real-time sampling and processing immediately fed into surround sound, all of which he remixed for the CD.

Wright’s collaborators on Cracked Glaze represent various facets of his work. Ensemble Klang, an ensemble of mostly Dutch new music virtuosi, was an early champion of Wright’s compositions. Spheric Totemic is a Wright-instigated, flexibly configured improvising group with, on this occasion, Mandhira de Saram, Alexander Hawkins, Neil Charles and Stephen Davis. Sofia Jernberg, whose Musho with Hawkins was one of the brighter lights of 2024, is new to Wright’s constellation.

Historically, the conventional wisdom among exponents of freely improvised music is that the larger the group, the more apt the music will be muddied. It is a yardstick that is also prevalent among practitioners of contemporary composition. Individuality – of the improviser, of the composer – is more difficult to assert in or through a crowd. Although there are more than a dozen musicians heard on Cracked Glaze, there is no nebulous sprawl or complexity for complexity’s sake. Abstraction is tethered to figuration, the spine of the piece being a descending line that repeatedly submerges and reemerges, giving the interactions of voices clear relationships.

“In a lot of my written work for ensembles there is a central concern that tends to last a long period of time, an idea that will give the piece structure. I’m really interested in music being a kind of terrain that you can hear through and around, so that when you are listening, you are experiencing a kind of ‘visual’ situation. I guess this goes back to my work with vinyl records, because records make music a physical surface, where you can place the needle anywhere in the terrain of the music.

“In the improvised work, I don’t want to be the guy that says to improvisers, ‘this is how it goes.’ Improvisation, in a free context, is about distributed leadership. It’s about this beautiful situation of people saying, ‘the music could go here’ or ‘I hear the future of this music in what you’re playing,’ and the kind of listening that leads to those sorts of situations.

“Having the opportunity to work with a group that is mainly readers – Ensemble Klang – and a group that is mainly improvisers – Spheric Totemic – and Sofia Jernberg, gave me the opportunity to do something I haven’t done much of in my music, to have a spine that is unfurling but is always there. It doesn’t necessarily always have to be the main focus of the piece, but it will always be there. It will structure time in a certain way; improvisers can do whatever they want to do, and the music will be as much about them as it is the spine. I was really interested in having a sort of ‘object’ in the space of the improvisation. It’s almost like in the visual art world, where you have people moving around in a gallery but there’s a sculpture there. It’s in the room with you.”

Another virtue of Cracked Glaze is that it is the type of work that initially seems to come out of nowhere. It smacks of singularity. However, Wright’s backstory reveals that he did not come out of nowhere, as he has a pedigree linking him to England’s most consequential institutional incubator of experimental music, as well as its most venerable, living exponent of improvised music. Both associations largely account for how Wright’s disparate interests – several of which were common among Gen Xers in their formative years but were delayed in being assimilated into experimental music – were shaped into a mature aesthetic, and yielded in Cracked Glaze an arguably definitive statement.

“My experience, first of all, was writing music and playing in brass bands and funk bands and small improvising groups with friends,” Wright recently explained. “But I also liked writing chamber music for people who would take it away and play it somewhere else. I might not even be there for the performance. This background took me to study at the University of Huddersfield with the Professor who set up the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival, Richard Steinitz. I was very lucky. It was kind of random. He was my composition teacher. So, I was very lucky to have experiences like knocking on the door for a composition lesson and Richard Steinitz saying, ‘Ah, Matt, I can’t possibly teach you right now, but meet Karlheinz,’ and the door opens and there’s this world-famous composer from another generation that I had read about, but never dreamed I would meet.

“Contemporary classical music was a big part of my education, but I DJed as a kid. I was really interested at that point in the ‘80s and ‘90s when software, sampling, and DJ technology, was becoming affordable. It started showing up in people’s homes. Contemporary classical music and DJ culture were colliding in my mind when I was a kid. The only kind of formal education I could get was a classical education, along with some jazz theory, but it was largely based on dot music, written music. Then there was this other (non-written) side, like DJ culture and all of the great heritage of Black music that DJ culture is part of, and that was a kind of informal education I studied for myself.

“When I was a real little kid – like 12 or 13 – I made a lot of bedroom productions with a basic computer and turntable setup, really focused on instrumental hip-hop. I started to scratch around then, just watching how it was done on TV. My main inspirations were DJ Premier of Gangstarr, Terminator X of Public Enemy, and Maseo of De La Soul. When I was around 18 or 19, as a student, I DJed for a few parties, playing mainly funk, hip hop, and drum ‘n' bass. Around the same time – 1996-98 – I was in a few pop/funk bands that needed a DJ, so I did a few things with beat juggling and matching the pitch of the horns with turntable scratches, etc.

“In 1999 I DJed for a social event at the Huddersfield Contemporary Music Festival and I decided to just play fragments of music that I loved at the time: The Jazz Warriors, Louis Andriessen, Loose Tubes, Squarepusher, Björk. On the basis of that weird mix, I got the call to DJ at Abbey Road for the launch of a music charity, the PRS Foundation, in 2000. That was both a social event and included some (not entirely successful!) experimental scratching. When I moved to Holland to study with composer Louis Andriessen in 2002, I joined a trio with laptop artist Tom Tlalim and saxophonist Keir Neuringer – now of Irreversible Entanglements – and we played a few house parties and small gigs with our own mix of free improv and beat-based electronica. That same year the Huddersfield Festival commissioned ‘Presents from an Edited Then’ which was a 70-minute piece for The Apollo Saxophone Quartet and me DJing, designed for a club venue, again a mix of ‘social’ and ‘experimental’. That’s when I got interested in the worlds of contemporary classical music and DJ culture colliding.”

One of the first projects Wright embarked on was to compose for turntables and to teach classically-trained percussionists how to use them, integrating John Cage’s early work for percussion with the innovations of Christian Marclay and Otomo Yoshihide. “In a piece called Contact Theatre I had literally written out all of the material for notation-reading percussionists”, Wright said of the work. “If you look at a musical stave with the four spaces between the lines, I used those spaces to represent the four spaces on a vinyl record. The space that would be a F in the treble stave, that’s the space on the outer edge of the record, before any musical material appears on the vinyl record. All of the musical material on the record is included in the second space, and then the space at the center of the record was the third space, and then the label itself in the fourth space. You can prepare those spaces, put stickers on them. I would literally write percussion rhythms and they could produce those rhythms by dropping the needle on the record and get a ricochet effect or specify a section of the record I want to be played, say a saxophone solo three minutes into the record. I developed these ‘half-contact’ techniques where the needle sticks like a locked groove, and I taught the basics of hip hop scratching to percussionists, even though the music didn’t sound anything like hip hop.”

Wright then began to assess the proportions of and the relationships between the elements of his aesthetic and how to integrate them in his work. “Cracked Glaze is a collision of all of the above. I have been doing ensemble work and turntable work and installation work, but a lot of my focus is on the work with Evan in mixing and even post-production of the Trance Map material. Post-production is really part of the process, and Evan is very interested in exploring all that. Although Cracked Glaze doesn’t involve Evan, it brings to equal terms all of the sources I work with. There’s some notation written for Ensemble Klang with holes in that notation, space for the improvisation group of Spheric Totemic and Sofia Jernberg. They have start and stop times for the improvising, and they also sometimes have cues for some notation. I’m also mixing them live on stage, taking samples and remixing them and using the turntable as well. Then I take all that material and work on it a little in the studio, not to radically change the piece but to bring out some of the elements that you would hear live but not in a stereo recording. The piece brings together notation, improvisation, and technology, but not as separate forms. They all intersect. That’s where they all join on the map.”

In a roundabout way, the title of the piece speaks to the processes of its creation. It refers to the glazes used in high-fire ceramics that are formulated to crack on temperature; even though they are applied in an even manner, the cracking results in a surface that can be likened to a mosaic assembled with random tiles, with dark, hair-thin spaces between them. Though the results are subject to a unique firing, the experienced artist knows how to promote cracking that is pleasing and avoid cracking that ruins the piece.

“It may be interesting to talk about how jazz standards have worked in the past,” Wright responded to the idea of controlled cracking, and chuckling at the notion that he controlled the gas valve. “An excellent standard is one that can be played in its entirety and feel integrated and beautiful, but it is also a catalyst. It offers itself up to be cracked, to be turned into something new. In some ways, the use of notation to suggest a response is fascinating to me. On a technical level, there are definitely moments where I say to the improvisers, ‘at a certain point you will hear a line and at that point, that pitch, that’s your moment; if you’re improvising, the natural ebb and flow of the group will go to you’. But I don’t say ‘you should crack it’ to them; I say ‘it’s yours’.

“And there’s a third element there, the equivalent of the heat – the processing and the spatialization. I’m taking the feed of everybody, the notated music and the improvised music is coming to my setup, and I’m able to remix it and sample it. I’m an agent in the cracking, too. Whether it is notated or not is not the point, because it’s all going through the same system and being splintered into surround sound. That’s the third element, the sound design is a catalytic element.”

Wright pointed to a poster in his studio of a still influential Japanese textile exhibition he attended in his early 20s. “What I loved about that,” he said, “was that the dynamic shapes of these textiles are very rigid, spatially, but the textiles themselves have all sorts of holes in them. They are almost like fishing nets. I tried to create something similar by creating a structure that’s flexible but has holes in it. If we play this piece again, the melody line and the structure is going to be exactly the same every time and the improvising and the specialization will be different every time. That’s a long-winded way of saying I tried not to over notate.”

Wright acknowledged that post-production, particularly when the work was created in a surround sound environment and is remixed for stereo, creates a distinct experience of the work, and perhaps represents a new iteration of the pursuit of perfection in the studio, exemplified by Glenn Gould. “My pieces are concepts that have a sort of quantum existence,” Wright maintained. “What I mean is that if we are going to present the piece live, then there are circumstances that will be dynamic for the audience in the live space that may not be so dynamic when hearing it at home. In the live space, I’m dealing with surround sound. There are a whole lot of options to try to present that sort of experience in the stereo format. When it comes to making a CD or something online that people will listen to, I consider the domestic setting. I also consider that many people listen to music on the go, with headphones or their phone. You may be walking down the Avenue of the Americas and everything around you is changing, but there’s one consistent thread in the music.

“You have to consider the multiple ways that people listen now. I do hope that people will sit at home to listen to it. In that situation, it’s much closer to reading a book because it’s a solitary experience. You’re sitting with it for 40 or 50 minutes. Wearing headphones creates an interior experience. I really treasure those kinds of listeners and it’s a real privilege when someone spends that time with something that I’ve made with my musical friends.

“In the history of improvised music there have been many vehement statements about the relationship between free improvised music and recording. I totally get that, but I suppose that the question we now have to consider is what happens when you improvise with a recording. We don’t want the karaoke thing! How does the recording come back into the improvised music experience in as fluid a way you would have with another musician with an instrument? An instrument is obviously a technology of its own and the recording is the result of the technology. We need to make sure the technology is as flexible as any other instrument. The other thing I’m really fascinated by in the history of free creative music is the evolution of incorporating electronics. It’s really interesting for me when an electro-acoustic improvised situation might suggest that the music is not happening in the present tense, but in the past or the future.

“The thing I’m really interested in is those previously separated camps of notation, improvisation, and technology becoming one and the same, where there is an equaling out of the three. You’re not relying on one form of expression. And this seems to be causing a real revitalization of the scene, where people are mastering their separate disciplines and are also negotiating with each other. I think there’s more opportunity for creative music because of the dialogue between notation, improvisation, and technology. Looking for the connections between them is the main creative impetus. It’s not paper; it’s not technology; it’s not adherence to one way of making music. It’s about thinking about the connections between the people you’re working with. Saying ‘all of the above’ may be too easy an answer, but it does ascribe equal value to notation, improvisation and technology. These are all zones on the map and they all overlap each other, so the paths between those zones are what I’m interested in.”

***

Wright’s projects frequently overlap, the post production of one coinciding with the development of another. With summer approaching, Wright was mixing a duo session with Pat Thomas that has the flavor of This is Trickster; a Spheric Totemic album, and a Trance Map + recording on which Parker and him are joined by harpist Milana Zaric and Richard Barrett.

The presence of Barrett is particularly intriguing, as he pioneered improvised electronic music beginning in the 1990s – largely through FURT, his partnership with Paul Obermayer – laying groundwork for Wright and others. Additionally, Barrett’s compositions are renowned for testing – and often surpassing – the presumed physical limits of instrumentalists.

Barrett and Wright are part of a trajectory of composers foregrounding technology in their work. An earlier dot on the line, one that is essential but not obvious, is Conlon Nancarrow. The expatriate composer is the inspiration for Wright’s next major work, “Passing Nancarrow.” Wright’s latest project with the Belgian ensemble BL!NDMAN (the exclamation point is intentional) also has Hawkins in a key role. The piece debuts next year, marking 30 years since Nancarrow died.

“The idea of the piece is based around Nancarrow being obsessed with Art Tatum’s playing,” Wright explained. “He sampled Tatum in the form of piano rolls, using technology from a hundred years ago. What we will do is, while Alex improvises in real time, his notes are captured and this will trigger all sorts of reactions from the group. In a way, we turn Alex’s music into a piano roll.”

Wright was partly inspired by the writer and documentary film director Helen Borton’s comment that jazz and blues collide like a “hurricane” in Nancarrow’s music. Replace “hurricane” with “Nancarrow” and you get the gist of Wright’s conceptualization for the recording he is currently mixing – “four hurricanes of all kinds of crazy sounds.” Wright also considered the music of Squarepusher, Aphex Twin, and other exponents of electronic dance music, that influenced him when Nancarrow died in 1997, leading him to include “strange, intelligent dance music in the piece.”

However, the nexus of Nancarrow, Barrett, and Wright, is the consideration of the limits of music humans can create in real time, and how to get to the edge of those limits, if not extend them.

“Nancarrow reached for impossible, post-human music. But in my current work, I don’t have an artistic interest in post-human AI. I’ve heard a lot of AI-generated music and read a lot of AI research, and the thing I’m already bored by is that AI can do almost anything. Like a musician that can play everything and just won’t stop playing to give space for others, AI doing anything and everything is boring to me when you don’t hear inspired choices and you don’t hear the human labor or the human need for considered space in the music. But, I’m open minded. I just haven’t heard anything that inspires me yet. Back to the human level, in Alex’s piano playing, there is that reaching beyond what is supposedly humanly possible, to reach a new vista for what is possible.

“You can say that, for his times, Nancarrow was making a post-human kind of music, but we should remember that he sat there, punching holes. So, I don’t hear a sort of pre-AI in his music, a piano that can do anything, but the blood and the hours of Nancarrow sitting maybe six months to create an explosive two minutes. I want to know how humans feel when they hear music and when they make music. If that is aided by technology, the idea is that the technology helps musical thinking like an instrument helps musical thinking. My interest in technology is the same as Alex’s interest in the piano, there’s a tradition of human tool use there that in a sense heightens the human listening experience if done successfully.

“Another thing I like about Nancarrow was that he was true to his beliefs, which is why he left the US for Mexico City, which resulted in him working in relative isolation. He just got on with it. A few people had experimented with the player piano before, but he made it his own. I appreciate that you can hear the edges in music and you’re OK with not being able to know everything beyond that edge. I guess the difference between the scene we have now and Nancarrow’s situation is that we can go to the edge together in a collaborative spirit.”
